final.title: Transcript Accuracy Is a Workflow Decision
final.body:
If transcript accuracy matters in your business, the useful question is not “is AI good enough?” It is: which recurring transcript task creates the most friction for you right now?

Treat it as a bounded workflow choice. First name the use case: customer-facing meeting notes, internal call summaries, or invoice line-item extraction. Each one has a different tolerance for error. Then write down two things for your own records: how long you spend checking it today, and what a single mistake would force you to correct. That gives you a real threshold instead of a vague sense that the transcript “looks fine.” Fine is not a control.

If the task is low risk, a draft may be enough. If it affects customer communication or approvals, keep a tighter human review step. For medical, legal, and high-sensitivity financial work, Bareni treats that as current scope discipline, not a casual automation target. Human approval stays mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

The next step is simple: choose one transcript workflow that repeats every week, note your current verification time or error rate, and use that as the starting point for the decision. If you cannot describe the threshold, you are not really reviewing accuracy; you are just hoping for the best.

final.title: Transcript Accuracy Is a Workflow Cost, Not a Feature
final.body:
If transcript accuracy matters to your business, the real question is not “is AI good enough?” It is: which recurring transcript task costs you more money and time today — manual checking, or accepting a draft that still needs review?

Treat accuracy as a bounded workflow decision. Separate the use case first: customer-facing meeting notes, internal call summaries, or text pulled from invoices and other records. Each one has a different tolerance for error. If the transcript feeds a high-risk decision, keep human approval in the loop. Money movement should stay human, and Bareni currently treats medical, legal, and high-sensitivity financial work as out of scope.

For a small business, the practical test is simple: pick one transcript task that repeats every week, then note two things for your own records — how long you spend verifying it, and what a single mistake would force you to fix. That gives you a real threshold instead of a vague feeling that “the transcript looked fine.” Fine is not a control.

If the task is low risk, a draft may be enough. If it is customer-facing or affects approvals, it needs a tighter review step. The next move is not to automate everything; it is to choose one workflow, write down the verification burden, and decide whether AI belongs in the draft stage or not. That is usually where the useful answer is hiding.
